key_takeaways: A legal elopement in Australia needs the two of you, an authorised celebrant and two witnesses over 18, all physically present, so plan for at least five people.
Give your Notice of Intended Marriage to your celebrant at least one month and no more than 18 months before the ceremony; a shorter notice period needs approval and is not automatic.

With a civil celebrant in Australia, the Marriage Act sets two passages (or words to that effect): the celebrant's monitum and the vow line each of you says to the other. The rest of the script can be your own, and your celebrant confirms the final wording.
A symbolic ceremony abroad can use any words you like, because the legal step happens separately, either at home first or under the destination's own law.
Short works best for two: a welcome, a few words about you, vows, rings and a pause with the view, then the signing.

faq.q: Can you elope with no witnesses in Australia?
faq.a: No. Section 44 of the Marriage Act 1961 says a marriage cannot be solemnised unless at least two people over 18 (or who appear to the celebrant to be over 18) are present as witnesses, and since 12 June 2024 they must be physically present with you and your celebrant.

faq.q: How long is an elopement ceremony?
faq.a: Personal vows of 250 to 300 words take about two minutes each, as our vows guide explains; time the rest by reading it aloud.

faq.q: Can we write our own words?
faq.a: Yes. At a legal ceremony in Australia with a civil celebrant, your own words sit alongside two passages the Marriage Act sets (or words to that effect): the celebrant's monitum and the vow line each of you says.

faq.q: Do we need a NOIM to elope?
faq.a: To marry legally in Australia, yes. You give a Notice of Intended Marriage to an authorised celebrant at least one month and no more than 18 months before the ceremony, and you can complete it while overseas.

faq.q: Can we elope abroad and have it recognised in Australia?
faq.a: Check before you book. Smartraveller says you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it took place and would have been valid under Australian law had it happened here. A symbolic ceremony is not a marriage, so this applies only to a legal ceremony. A legal marriage abroad follows the destination's law, so start with that country's registry or embassy and confirm the steps for your passports. Our guide to overseas marriage certificates explains what happens to the paperwork afterwards.
